facts.fact: The East India Company came to India in 1600 under a charter of Queen Elizabeth I.
In 1765 the Company acquired the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, becoming a territorial power.
After the revolt of 1857 the Crown took direct control of India in 1858.
The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first step of the British Government to regulate the Company.
The Regulating Act 1773 recognised the political and administrative functions of the Company.
The Regulating Act 1773 created the Governor-General of Bengal; Warren Hastings was the first.
The Regulating Act provided an Executive Council of four members to assist the Governor-General.
The Regulating Act made the Governors of Bombay and Madras subordinate to the Governor-General of Bengal.
The Regulating Act provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774.
The Calcutta Supreme Court had one Chief Justice and three judges; Elijah Impey was the first Chief Justice.
The Regulating Act prohibited Company servants from private trade and from accepting bribes.
Under the Regulating Act the Court of Directors had to report revenue, civil and military affairs to the British Government.
The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) exempted the Governor-General and Council from Supreme Court jurisdiction for official acts.
The Act of Settlement 1781 excluded revenue matters from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
The Act of Settlement 1781 required the court to respect the personal law of Hindus and Muslims.
Pitt's India Act 1784 created the Board of Control for political affairs.
Pitt's India Act left commercial affairs with the Court of Directors and so set up a double government.
Pitt's India Act first called the Company's territories the 'British possessions in India'.
The Charter Act of 1793 extended the Company's trade monopoly for 20 years.
The Charter Act 1793 let the Governor-General override his Council and the Bombay and Madras governments.
The Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except in tea and the trade with China.
The Charter Act 1813 asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's territories.
The Charter Act 1813 did not place Indian revenues under the British Parliament.
The Charter Act 1813 allowed Christian missionaries into India.
The Charter Act 1813 earmarked Rs 1 lakh for education (Western education).
The Charter Act 1813 empowered local governments to impose taxes.
The Charter Act 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India; Lord William Bentinck was the first.
The Charter Act 1833 was the final step towards centralisation, giving exclusive legislative power to the Governor-General of India.
Laws made before 1833 were called Regulations and those under the 1833 Act were called Acts.
The Charter Act 1833 ended the Company's commercial activities, making it a purely administrative body.
The 1833 Act's attempt at open competition for civil services was negated after the Court of Directors opposed it.
The Charter Act 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
The Charter Act 1853 was the last of the Charter Acts.
The 1853 Act created the Indian (Central) Legislative Council, which worked as a mini-Parliament.
The Charter Act 1853 introduced open competition for the ICS, open to Indians.
The Macaulay Committee on the Indian Civil Service was appointed in 1854.
The 1853 Act extended Company rule without fixing any period.
The 1853 Act introduced local representation, with four members from Madras, Bombay, Bengal and Agra.
The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the Crown.
The 1858 Act was known as the Act for the Good Government of India.
The 1858 Act redesignated the Governor-General as the Viceroy; Lord Canning was the first Viceroy.
The 1858 Act created the Secretary of State for India, a member of the British Cabinet.
The Secretary of State was assisted by a 15-member Council of India.
The 1858 Act ended double government by abolishing the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation was issued on 1 November 1858.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation disclaimed any intention to annex the princely States.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation placed Indian administration under the British Crown and did not regulate Company trade.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised religious toleration.
The Indian Councils Act 1861 began associating Indians (non-officials) with law-making.
In 1862 Lord Canning nominated the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao to the Legislative Council.
The 1861 Act began decentralisation by restoring legislative powers to Bombay and Madras.
New legislative councils followed in Bengal (1862), the North-Western Provinces (1866) and Punjab (1897).
The 1861 Act gave statutory recognition to Lord Canning's portfolio system (1859).
The 1861 Act empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances in an emergency, valid for six months.
The Indian Councils Act 1892 let councils discuss the budget and question the executive.
The 1892 Act increased the number of non-official members in the councils.
The 1892 Act provided limited, indirect election through recommendations of district boards, universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.
The Indian Councils Act 1909 is named after Lord Morley (Secretary of State) and Lord Minto (Viceroy).
The Morley-Minto Reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
Lord Minto is called the 'Father of Communal Electorate'.
Satyendra Prasad Sinha was the first Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council (Law Member), under the 1909 Act.
The 1909 Act enlarged the Central Legislative Council from 16 to 60 members.
The 1909 Act let members ask supplementary questions and move resolutions on the budget.
The Government of India Act 1919 is named after Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy).
Montagu's August Declaration of 20 August 1917 promised responsible government and led to the 1919 Act.
The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces — transferred and reserved subjects.
Under 1919 dyarchy, Administration of Justice, Land Revenue and Police were Reserved subjects.
Under 1919 dyarchy, Local Self-Government was a Transferred subject.
The 1919 Act clearly demarcated central and provincial subjects (jurisdiction).
The 1919 Act introduced bicameralism at the Centre and direct elections.
The 1919 Act required three of the six members of the Viceroy's Executive Council (other than the C-in-C) to be Indians.
The 1919 Act extended communal representation to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.
The 1919 Act created the office of the High Commissioner for India in London.
The 1919 Act provided for a Public Service Commission; the Central PSC was set up in 1926.
The 1919 Act separated provincial budgets from the central budget.
The 1919 Act granted franchise on the basis of property, tax or education.
The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms did not recommend voting rights for all women above 21.
The Simon Commission was boycotted because it had no Indian member.
The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927 with seven British members and reported in 1930.
Three Round Table Conferences (1930-32) were held; Ramsay MacDonald's Communal Award (1932) was modified by the Poona Pact.
The Butler Committee (1927) examined relations between the Government of India and the princely States.
The Government of India Act 1935 had 321 sections and 10 Schedules.
The 1935 Act proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and princely States, which never came into being.
The 1935 Act divided powers into Federal (59), Provincial (54) and Concurrent (36) lists.
Under the 1935 Act residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General.
The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced provincial autonomy.
The 1935 Act provided for dyarchy at the Centre, which never came into operation.
The 1935 Act introduced bicameralism in six of the eleven provinces.
The 1935 Act extended communal representation to the depressed classes, women and labour.
The 1935 Act gave women reserved seats in the legislatures.
The 1935 Act extended the franchise to about 10 per cent of the population.
The 1935 Act abolished the Council of India.
The 1935 Act provided for the Reserve Bank of India and federal, provincial and joint Public Service Commissions.
The 1935 Act set up a Federal Court, established in 1937.
The 1935 Act separated Burma from India.
The structural part of the Constitution is largely based on the Government of India Act 1935.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 created two dominions, India and Pakistan.
The 1947 Act abolished the office of Viceroy and provided a Governor-General for each dominion appointed on its cabinet's advice.
The 1947 Act made each Constituent Assembly sovereign and empowered it to frame a constitution.
The 1947 Act let princely States join India or Pakistan or remain independent, as paramountcy lapsed.
The 1947 Act abolished the office of Secretary of State for India.
The Indian Independence Act was based on the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.
The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947, after Attlee's announcement of 20 February 1947.
C. Rajagopalachari was the last Governor-General of India, and Mountbatten the first after independence.
The Nehru Report (1928), by Motilal Nehru and eight others, was the first major Indian attempt at a constitution.
The Karachi session of the Congress (1931) passed a resolution on Fundamental Rights and economic policy.
M.N. Roy first proposed a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
The Congress officially demanded a Constituent Assembly in 1935.
In 1938 Nehru declared the Assembly must be elected on adult franchise without outside interference.
The August Offer of 1940 (Linlithgow) accepted the demand for a Constituent Assembly in principle.
The Cripps Mission (1942) proposed a Constituent Assembly after the Second World War; the Muslim League rejected it.
Under the Cripps proposals a province not accepting the new Constitution could sign a separate agreement with Britain.
Cripps did not propose an Assembly wholly nominated by the Governor-General — members were to be elected by provincial assemblies with princely nominees.
The Constituent Assembly was constituted in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
The Cabinet Mission recommended a federal government with grouping of provinces, not larger court powers or more Indians in the ICS.
The Cabinet Mission members were Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.
The Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946 with Nehru at its head.
The Constituent Assembly was to have 389 seats: 292 provinces, 4 Chief Commissioners' provinces and 93 princely States.
After partition the Assembly's strength fell to 299.
Seats were allotted roughly one per 10 lakh people.
Provincial seats were divided among Muslims, Sikhs and the General community by population.
Provincial members were indirectly elected by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies by proportional representation and single transferable vote.
Princely-State representatives were nominated by the heads of the States, so the Assembly was partly elected and partly nominated.
Elections to the Assembly were held in July 1946.
In the 1946 election the Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and others 15.
The Assembly first met on 9 December 1946.
The first meeting was attended by 211 members.
The Muslim League boycotted the first meeting.
Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President of the Assembly.
Sinha was made temporary President as the oldest member, following the French practice.
Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946.
H.C. Mukherjee and V.T. Krishnamachari were the two Vice-Presidents of the Assembly.
B.N. Rau was the Constitutional Advisor of the Assembly.
The Assembly met in the Constitution Hall, now the Central Hall of Parliament.
The Objectives Resolution was moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946.
The Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947.
The ideals of the Objectives Resolution became the Preamble, its philosophical foundation.
On 28 April 1947 representatives of six princely States took their seats in the Assembly.
After the Independence Act the Assembly became a sovereign body and also the first legislature of free India.
When the Assembly met as the legislature it was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar.
The Assembly adopted the national flag on 22 July 1947.
The Assembly ratified India's Commonwealth membership in May 1949.
The Assembly adopted the national anthem and national song on 24 January 1950.
On 24 January 1950 the Assembly elected Rajendra Prasad the first President of India.
284 members signed the Constitution on 24 January 1950, the Assembly's final session.
From 26 January 1950 the Assembly acted as the provisional Parliament until the 1951-52 elections.
About 7,635 amendments to the draft were proposed and 2,473 discussed.
The Draft Constitution was published in February 1948.
The third reading of the draft ran from 14 to 26 November 1949.
The Assembly held 11 sessions.
Making the Constitution took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.
Making the Constitution cost about Rs 64 lakh.
The makers studied the constitutions of about 60 countries.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.
The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
Provisions on citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament and transitional matters came into force on 26 November 1949.
26 January was chosen to honour Purna Swaraj Day of 1930.
The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.
On 26 January 1950 India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; Socialist and Secular came with the 42nd Amendment (1976).
The original Constitution was handwritten by Prem Behari Narain Raizada.
Vasant Krishan Vaidya calligraphed the Hindi version, and Nandalal Bose decorated the pages.
The elephant was the symbol (seal) of the Constituent Assembly.
About 15 women were members of the Constituent Assembly.
B.R. Ambedkar is called the Father of the Constitution.
The Supreme Court is the custodian of the Constitution.
The Assembly had 8 major and 15 minor committees.
The Union Powers Committee was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The Union Constitution Committee was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The States Committee (for negotiating with the States) was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
The Provincial Constitution Committee was chaired by Sardar Patel.
The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas was chaired by Sardar Patel.
The Rules of Procedure Committee was chaired by Rajendra Prasad.
The Steering Committee was chaired by Rajendra Prasad.
The Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee was chaired by J.B. Kripalani.
The Minorities Sub-Committee was chaired by H.C. Mukherjee.
The North-East Frontier Tribal Areas and Assam Excluded Areas Sub-Committee was chaired by Gopinath Bardoloi.
The Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas (other than Assam) Sub-Committee was chaired by A.V. Thakkar.
The Finance and Staff Committee and the Ad-hoc Committee on the National Flag were chaired by Rajendra Prasad.
The Credentials Committee was chaired by Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar.
The House Committee was chaired by B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The Order of Business Committee was chaired by K.M. Munshi.
The Committee on the Functions of the Constituent Assembly was chaired by G.V. Mavalankar.
The Ad-hoc Committee on the Supreme Court was chaired by S. Varadachari.
The Committee on Chief Commissioners' Provinces was chaired by Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
The Expert Committee on Financial Provisions was chaired by Nalini Ranjan Ghosh.
The Linguistic Provinces Commission was chaired by S.K. Dhar.
The Special Committee to examine the Draft Constitution was chaired by Nehru.
The Press Gallery Committee was chaired by Usha Nath Sen.
The Drafting Committee was chaired by B.R. Ambedkar.
The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947.
The Drafting Committee had seven members.
Members included N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi and Syed Mohammad Saadullah.
Syed Mohammad Saadullah was a member of the Drafting Committee.
N. Madhava Rau replaced B.L. Mitter on the Drafting Committee.
T.T. Krishnamachari replaced D.P. Khaitan, who died in 1948.
Nehru and Rajendra Prasad were not members of the Drafting Committee.
B.N. Rau prepared the first draft of the Constitution in October 1947.
The office of Governor, Public Service Commissions and emergency provisions come from the GoI Act 1935.
Parliamentary government, rule of law and single citizenship are borrowed from the UK.
The cabinet system and bicameralism are borrowed from the UK.
Prerogative writs and parliamentary privileges are borrowed from the UK.
Fundamental Rights and judicial review are borrowed from the USA.
Impeachment of the President, removal of judges and the post of Vice-President are borrowed from the USA.
Independence of the judiciary is borrowed from the USA.
Directive Principles of State Policy are borrowed from Ireland.
Nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha and the method of electing the President come from Ireland.
A federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Centre are borrowed from Canada.
Appointment of state Governors by the Centre and the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court come from Canada.
The Concurrent List, joint sitting and freedom of trade and commerce are borrowed from Australia.
Suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency is borrowed from Weimar Germany.
Fundamental Duties and the ideal of justice in the Preamble are borrowed from the USSR.
The republic and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity come from France.
The procedure for amendment and election of Rajya Sabha members come from South Africa.
Procedure established by law is borrowed from Japan.
The philosophical part (FRs and DPSP) comes from the American and Irish constitutions; the political part from the British.
Vallabhbhai Patel held Home and I&B in the Interim Government, led the Bardoli satyagraha and integrated the princely States.
Abul Kalam Azad later became the first Education Minister.
Rajendra Prasad was known for the Champaran Satyagraha and was three times Congress President.
H.C. Mookherjee later became Governor of West Bengal.
Durgabai Deshmukh founded the Andhra Mahila Sabha and later chaired the Central Social Welfare Board.
Baldev Singh, a Panthic Akali leader, later became Defence Minister.
K.M. Munshi was later a founder of the Swatantra Party.
Ambedkar was the first Law Minister and is linked with the Republican Party of India.
Shyama Prasad Mukherjee, Minister for Industry and Supply, founded the Bharatiya Jana Sangh.
Sarojini Naidu later became Governor of Uttar Pradesh.
Somnath Lahiri was a Communist Party of India leader in the Assembly.
Andhra members of the Assembly included Durgabai Deshmukh, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N.G. Ranga and Tanguturi Prakasam.
Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, a Drafting Committee member, was born in Nellore district of Andhra.
The national flag adopted on 22 July 1947 was based on the design of Pingali Venkayya.
